$comment: The 28 steps of one CLPR round trip as the protocol specifies them. `steps` is the Hiero -> EVM (QBFT) direction; `reverse` is EVM -> Hiero. The phases are shared. `plain` is the non-technical narration; `protocol` is the precise version. `lit` lists the diagram nodes that are active at that step. Refs point into clpr-spec (see sources.json).

phases.title: Getting in line
phases.plain: Everything here happens inside one transaction on the sending ledger. If any check fails, the whole thing is thrown out and nothing was sent.

phases.title: Proving it happened
phases.plain: The endpoints get involved. Nothing is submitted to either chain.

phases.title: Crossing
phases.plain: One ordinary transaction on the receiving ledger. Everything from the proof check to the queued reply happens inside it.

phases.title: Coming home
phases.plain: The reply travels back. The proof works completely differently in this direction; the rules about the message do not.

phases.title: Closing the loop
phases.plain: The original sender hears back, and its message is cleared from the queue.

steps.label: sendMessage()
steps.title: The application calls sendMessage on the CLPR Service
steps.plain: One function call from the application to its CLPR Service. It hands over four things: which channel to use, which connector is paying, who the message is for, and the message itself. The application does no cross-ledger work of its own; it passes all of that to the CLPR Service and gets back a message id.
steps.protocol: The application calls sendMessage on the Hiero CLPR Service with the channel id, the connector id, the target application and the message data. Any caller can send. The CLPR Service sets the message's sender to the caller's address, never to a value the caller supplies, and on success returns the new message id, which the application uses to match the eventual reply.

steps.label: channel checks
steps.title: Channel ACTIVE; payload and queue-depth checks
steps.plain: Before accepting anything, the CLPR Service checks the obvious. Does this channel exist and is it active? Is the message small enough for the other ledger to accept? Is the outbound queue already full? Any "no" and the call is rejected with nothing changed.
steps.protocol: Enqueue rejects the send, with no change to state, if the channel does not exist or is not ACTIVE, if the message's payload bytes exceed the peer's published payload limit, or if the outbound queue would then hold more messages the peer has not acknowledged than the local queue depth allows, counting any ConfigUpdate enqueued with it.

steps.label: quota
steps.title: Per-connector queue quota
steps.plain: One busy connector could fill a shared outbound queue and block every other connector on the channel. The recommended defence is to give each connector its own share of the queue and to reject a send once that share is used up.
steps.protocol: A recommendation, not a protocol rule: the CLPR Service limits each connector to a fixed share of the local queue depth, in addition to the channel-wide depth check of enqueue. On Hiero the count is the connector's DATA messages above the stored acknowledgement, and a quota of zero disables the check.

steps.label: authorization
steps.title: The connector authorizes the message
steps.plain: The connector is the account that pays. The CLPR Service asks it, in effect: are you willing to cover this one? If it says no, nothing is sent.
steps.protocol: The connector named in the send must be registered on the channel, and the CLPR Service calls its contract's authorization function with the channel, the target application, the sender and the message data. Anything but true rejects the send. By returning true the source connector commits that its counterpart on the destination can pay for executing the message, and that it can cover the cost of handling the reply. That commitment is the basis of the recommended slashing.

steps.label: config sync
steps.title: A ConfigUpdate is queued first if this ledger's settings changed
steps.plain: If this ledger's configuration changed since it was last sent on this channel, a ConfigUpdate is put in the queue ahead of the message. On a normal day nothing has changed and this step does nothing.
steps.protocol: Enqueue step 1: when a ConfigUpdate is due on the channel, because the configuration changed after the last one propagated on it, the CLPR Service enqueues a CONTROL ConfigUpdate carrying its full configuration before the DATA message. Its place in the queue is fixed by consensus, so both ledgers agree on the point in the stream where the new limits apply.

steps.label: enqueue
steps.title: Message stored, running hash chained, next id advanced
steps.plain: The message is written into the outbound queue and given the next number in line. It is also folded into a running hash of everything sent on this channel, so the other ledger can later check that nothing was inserted, removed or reordered.
steps.protocol: The DATA message is built with the connector id, the target application, the message data and the caller as sender, and appended to the outbound queue under the next message id. Its running hash is computed over its canonical protobuf payload bytes, chained onto the previous running hash; the sent running hash is set to it and the next message id advances. Both ledgers hash the same bytes, so the receiver can recompute the chain.

steps.label: threshold signature
steps.title: The Hiero network signs the block root
steps.plain: The sending ledger's consensus nodes jointly sign block roots with a single threshold signature, which counts only if nodes holding more than half of the consensus weight took part. The endpoint proves the message from the state at the start of a later directly signed block, and a signed block is final.
steps.protocol: Hiero nodes sign block roots with a hinTS threshold signature, valid only from nodes holding more than half of the consensus weight of the roster its verification key commits to. The endpoint proves from the starting state of a block whose root is signed directly; a block that is final only because a later block was signed gives no snapshot, and the proven state cannot be reverted. For a channel to an EVM ledger the Hiero endpoint uses the hinTS proof scheme, whose trust anchor is the current hinTS verification key.

steps.label: gRPC open
steps.title: A sync stream opens and BundleRequests are exchanged
steps.plain: An endpoint of one ledger opens a sync session with an endpoint of the other. Each side says which message it has reached, so the other knows exactly what to send.
steps.protocol: A sync cycle is one new bidirectional gRPC stream for one channel, opened by an initiator to an endpoint chosen from the peer manifest. Each side first sends a BundleRequest with its received message id, its channel status, the id of the trust anchor it holds and the manifest version it holds; each then answers the other with at most one bundle. Under the specification the stream runs over TLS when the responder's manifest entry carries a certificate, in plaintext otherwise, with no fallback and no client certificate; the reference endpoint serves it in plaintext. The request is unproven: it only shapes the bundle and never changes state. Delivery is pulled, not pushed.

steps.label: gather proof
steps.title: The Hiero endpoint gathers the bundle and its proof
steps.plain: The endpoint reads the messages and the proof that they really are in the ledger's signed state. It only collects this proof; the signature in it is the ledger's, and the endpoint could not forge it.
steps.protocol: The endpoint reads all bundle content from one signed snapshot, the starting state of a directly signed block. The run starts after the requestor's received message id and stays within the peer's message count and size limits and the scheme's path limits. The proof is a Merkle path to the block root for the channel record and for each message, under the block's compact hinTS signature.

steps.label: gRPC send
steps.title: The BundleResponse travels down the stream
steps.plain: The messages, together with their proof, travel down the open stream to the other ledger's endpoint.
steps.protocol: A BundleResponse carries one opaque bundle in the wire layout of the source's proof scheme: the proven queue metadata, a contiguous run of messages, and the proven id and running hash of the last one. Proving the last running hash and recomputing the chain binds every message in the run. A bundle may end before the sender's latest message, and may carry no messages at all.

steps.label: pre-verify
steps.title: The EVM endpoint dry-runs the submission
steps.plain: Under the recommended practice, before paying to submit anything, the receiving endpoint checks that the bundle would be accepted, by a read-only preview. A bundle the ledger rejects still costs its submitter the transaction fee.
steps.protocol: Recommended practice: the receiving endpoint checks the progress criteria against its last view of the channel and previews the submission read-only. On EVM ledgers it previews every submission against pending state and skips any bundle that would revert. A rejected bundle still costs the submitter its transaction fee.

steps.label: submitBundle()
steps.title: The bundle lands on the EVM CLPR Service
steps.plain: The endpoint sends an ordinary transaction on the destination ledger carrying the bundle. Everything from here until the reply is queued happens inside this single transaction.
steps.protocol: Any account may call submitBundle with the channel id and the bundle; submission is permissionless. Processing is atomic: a bundle rejected at any step changes nothing and costs the submitter its fee. Under the recommended design, the submitter receives every execution charge and slash penalty the bundle produces; if that transfer fails, the CLPR Service may pay its administrator instead, and on EVM ledgers a last fallback credits the submitter a pending withdrawal.

steps.label: verifyBundle()
steps.title: The verifier checks the threshold signature and the Merkle paths
steps.plain: The verifier checks the Hiero nodes' joint signature and the proof paths against the signing key on record for this channel. If the network's roster has changed since, the bundle also proves the chain of keys from the recorded one to the new one. The endpoints that carried the bundle are trusted for none of it.
steps.protocol: The CLPR Service calls the channel's verifier with the bundle, the stored trust anchor and the channel context; the call is read-only and the verifier keeps no per-channel state. Under the hinTS proof scheme the trust anchor names one hinTS verification key. The verifier checks the Merkle paths to the block root of the channel record, the last message and, when present, the endpoint manifest; the earlier messages are bound by the running hash. It checks the threshold signature on that root, which counts only from nodes holding more than half of the consensus weight. A bundle signed under a later key carries a provenance chain, each key signed by its predecessor; the verifier then returns a trust anchor change, stored before any message is processed. It returns the queue metadata, the messages, and the last message's id and running hash.

steps.label: hash chain
steps.title: Progress, size, replay and running-hash checks
steps.plain: Then the bookkeeping. Does the bundle bring anything new? Do its messages follow on from the last one received, with no gap? Messages already received are skipped. Does recomputing the running hash give the proven value? Any mismatch and the whole bundle is rejected.
steps.protocol: Bundle processing then checks, in order: the bundle's message count and each DATA payload are within the destination's own limits, its size having been checked before the verifier was called; at least one progress criterion holds; any new endpoint manifest and trust anchor are installed; the message range has no gap, and messages already received are skipped; the running hash recomputed from the stored received running hash over the new messages equals the proven running hash of the last one; and the acknowledgement neither moves backwards nor covers a message never sent. These are the CLPR Service's own checks; they catch verifier bugs, not a compromised verifier.

steps.label: gas budget
steps.title: Connector resolved and the gas budget computed
steps.plain: The destination looks up the connector that agreed to pay, checks it can pay, and works out how much execution it can afford.
steps.protocol: The message's connector id resolves to the connector registered with that id on the channel. If none exists the outcome is CONNECTOR_NOT_FOUND; if it cannot pay, CONNECTOR_UNDERFUNDED, and the application is not called. Both are replies, not bundle failures. The execution budget is at most the destination's per-message gas limit; on EVM ledgers it is reduced to what the connector's balance can pay for. Recommended slashing: none for a missing connector, whose cost the submitter absorbs; the local connector for one that cannot pay.

steps.label: onClprMessage()
steps.title: The application receives the message and answers it
steps.plain: The application on the other ledger receives the message, does its work and returns its answer. This is the moment the message has actually crossed; everything before it was transport.
steps.protocol: The CLPR Service calls the target application's onClprMessage with the channel id, the sender and the message data, within the execution budget. Returned bytes become the reply with status SUCCESS. A revert, a target that is not an application, or return data that is not bytes gives APPLICATION_ERROR, as does a reply too large for the peer. A failing application affects only its own reply, never the bundle.

steps.label: settle gas
steps.title: The connector is charged and the submitter reimbursed
steps.plain: Under the recommended design, the connector pays for the execution that just happened, plus a margin, and the whole amount goes to whoever submitted the bundle. The margin covers the submitter's overhead and gives it a reason to submit.
steps.protocol: Recommended charging: for each dispatched DATA message the destination connector pays the execution cost plus a margin, one value for the whole CLPR Service, and all of it goes to the bundle submitter. No share goes to the Service or its administrator, except as the fallback when the transfer fails. On EVM ledgers the cost is the gas the application used at the transaction's gas price, collected after dispatch; a failed charge slashes the connector and leaves the reply's status unchanged.

steps.label: reply queued
steps.title: The reply is enqueued as a REPLY message
steps.plain: The answer is placed in the destination ledger's own outbound queue, numbered and folded into the running hash the same way the original was. Every DATA message receives exactly one reply, even when the connector was missing or could not pay.
steps.protocol: A REPLY carrying the original message id, the status and the reply data is appended to the destination's outbound queue and chained into its sent running hash, before the next message of the bundle is processed. Every DATA message receives exactly one REPLY, in the order of the DATA messages.

steps.label: received id
steps.title: The destination records how far it has received
steps.plain: The destination records how far it has now received. The other ledger reads that number, proven, in the next bundle sent back, and uses it to know what it can safely delete.
steps.protocol: After dispatch the destination's received message id and received running hash advance to the bundle's last message. They are part of the shared channel state, so the next bundle in the other direction proves them as queue metadata, and the source takes that received message id as its acknowledgement. The reference contracts also emit an event when a bundle is processed in full.

steps.label: QBFT proof
steps.title: The EVM endpoint builds a QBFT state proof
steps.plain: Coming back, the proof works differently. This ledger's validators seal each block header directly, so the endpoint takes a sealed header and a proof of the contract storage holding the channel's state; the reply is tied to that state by the running hash. If the validators have changed, it also carries the evidence of that change.
steps.protocol: The EVM endpoint reads one sealed block, which QBFT makes final, and builds every proof at it: the block header with its QBFT committed seals, the material that carries the validator set across any change since the peer's trust anchor, an account proof of the CLPR Service and storage proofs of the channel's state and, for a partial bundle, of the last message's running hash. The validator-change material depends on the channel's QBFT proof scheme: sealed headers at which the set changes, or proofs of a validator contract's storage.

steps.label: gRPC back
steps.title: Delivery to the Hiero endpoint, then pre-verification
steps.plain: The reply exists only once the destination has processed the message, so a later sync carries it back. The receiving Hiero node is expected to check it before submitting it.
steps.protocol: A later sync cycle carries the REPLY back. Recommended practice on Hiero: the receiving node checks every bundle before submitting it, for the channel status, the size, local verification, the trust anchor and progress, and skips a bundle that makes no progress.

steps.label: node submits
steps.title: Bundle submission on the Hiero ledger
steps.plain: The Hiero node that received the reply submits it to its own ledger, in a transaction of that ledger's own API rather than an EVM one.
steps.protocol: Recommended practice on Hiero: the receiving node submits the bundle as a node transaction paid by its node account, and the native CLPR Service runs the same bundle processing algorithm. The node is the submitter, so it receives the charges and penalties the bundle produces.

steps.label: verify seals
steps.title: QBFT committed seals checked against the trust anchor
steps.plain: The Hiero ledger checks the validator seals on that block header against the validators it holds for this channel, and follows any change of validators since. A quorum of the trusted validators must have sealed it: two thirds when the set is unchanged.
steps.protocol: The channel's verifier on Hiero recovers the signers of the header's QBFT committed seals and requires a quorum of the trusted validator set among them, two thirds when the set is unchanged. When the set has changed since the trust anchor, the bundle carries the change: under the QBFT header scheme, each header at which the listed set changes, moving it by at most one member; under the QBFT contract scheme, each block at which the validator contract's set changes. Each must be sealed by enough of the set trusted before it, so history cannot be skipped; under the QBFT header scheme a header that changes the set by one member can need one signer fewer. The new set is returned as a trust anchor change.

steps.label: verify state
steps.title: Account and storage proofs, then replay and running-hash checks
steps.plain: Then it checks the proof tying the reply to that exact sealed block, and repeats the same sequence and running hash checks as the outbound leg. The proof technology differs; the rules do not.
steps.protocol: The account proof ties the CLPR Service contract, and its code hash, to the sealed header's state root; the storage proofs tie the channel's proven state, and for a partial bundle the last message's running hash, to that account. Every value comes from the one sealed block. The CLPR Service then runs the same processing steps as on the outbound leg: limits, progress, replay defence, running hash and acknowledgement. Only the proof scheme changes.

steps.label: ordering
steps.title: Response ordering verified against the retained message
steps.plain: Replies have to come back in the order the messages went out. If one arrives out of turn, nothing in that bundle is delivered and the channel pauses. It resumes by itself once a bundle arrives in the right order.
steps.protocol: Every REPLY must answer the oldest unanswered DATA message in the outbound queue; the walk skips REPLY and CONTROL entries. A mismatch is a response ordering violation: nothing in the bundle is dispatched, an ACTIVE channel becomes PAUSED, and sends are rejected while queued messages keep syncing. The bundle's manifest and trust anchor changes still apply, and the CLPR Service may also apply its acknowledgement. The first bundle accepted without a violation returns the channel to ACTIVE.

steps.label: onClprResponse()
steps.title: The original application is called back
steps.plain: The original application is called back with the message id, a status, and whatever the other side sent back.
steps.protocol: The CLPR Service delivers the message id, the status and the reply data to the application that sent the DATA message, through its onClprResponse callback. The status is SUCCESS, APPLICATION_ERROR, CONNECTOR_NOT_FOUND or CONNECTOR_UNDERFUNDED. Delivery is best effort: a failing callback does not affect processing of the REPLY, and on Hiero the callback is skipped when the source connector cannot prepay its gas. Under the recommended policy, a CONNECTOR_NOT_FOUND or CONNECTOR_UNDERFUNDED reply slashes the source connector.

steps.label: delivered
steps.title: Reply delivered; the original message deleted
steps.plain: Only now is the original message deleted from the outbound queue. It was deliberately kept until its reply arrived, so the ordering check just before had something to compare against.
steps.protocol: DATA messages are kept after acknowledgement because response ordering is checked against them; a DATA message is deleted when its REPLY is processed. REPLY and CONTROL messages, by contrast, are deleted as soon as they are acknowledged.

steps.label: complete
steps.title: Round trip complete
steps.plain: A message went to another ledger, ran there, and its answer came back. Each leg carried a proof of the other ledger's own consensus, checked on arrival by the channel's verifier, with no intermediary network or bridge validator set in the middle.
steps.protocol: Two bundles, two proofs, two verifications, one reply. The application trusted its own ledger's consensus and CLPR Service, the channel's verifier, the peer ledger's consensus and CLPR Service, and the remote application. Delivery also depended on at least one honest endpoint on each side and a connector that pays.

reverse.label: sendMessage()
reverse.title: The EVM application calls sendMessage on its CLPR Service
reverse.plain: The same call, started from the other side. The application on the EVM ledger hands the four things (channel, connector, recipient, message) to its CLPR Service contract and gets back a message id.
reverse.protocol: The EVM application calls sendMessage on the CLPR Service contract, with the Hiero application's address as the target application. The CLPR Service sets the sender to the caller's address and returns the message id.

reverse.label: channel checks
reverse.title: Channel ACTIVE; payload and queue-depth checks
reverse.plain: The same checks as the other direction, this time in a smart contract rather than inside the node. Channel active, message small enough, outbound queue not full.
reverse.protocol: The same enqueue checks: the channel ACTIVE, the payload within the peer's published payload limit, and the unacknowledged messages within the local queue depth. The peer's limits are the throttles stored with the channel at setup and replaced by each ConfigUpdate the peer sends.

reverse.label: quota
reverse.title: Connector queue quota checked
reverse.plain: Under the recommended design, the connector's share of the outbound queue is checked, so one connector cannot fill the queue for everyone.
reverse.protocol: A recommendation, not a protocol rule: each connector is limited to a fixed share of the local queue depth. On EVM ledgers the count is the connector's DATA messages from enqueue until their REPLY arrives, and a send is rejected once the connector is at its quota.

reverse.label: authorization
reverse.title: The connector authorizes the message
reverse.plain: The connector on this side approves the message. The same connector is registered on both ledgers under one id: it approves the message here and pays for it on the other side.
reverse.protocol: The CLPR Service calls the connector contract's authorization function with the channel, the target application, the sender and the message data. The connector id is derived from the channel id, the operator's public key and a salt, so an operator who registers with the same key and salt on both ledgers gets the same id on both, and the destination resolves that connector to pay.

reverse.label: config sync
reverse.title: A ConfigUpdate is queued first if this ledger's settings changed
reverse.plain: If this ledger's configuration changed since it was last sent on this channel, a ConfigUpdate is put in the queue ahead of the message. When nothing has changed, this step is skipped.
reverse.protocol: Enqueue step 1: when a ConfigUpdate is due on the channel, because the configuration changed after the last one propagated on it, the CLPR Service enqueues a CONTROL ConfigUpdate carrying its full configuration before the DATA message. Its place in the queue is fixed by consensus, so both ledgers agree on the point in the stream where the new limits apply.

reverse.label: enqueue
reverse.title: Message stored, running hash chained, next id advanced
reverse.plain: The message is written into the outbound queue and folded into the running hash, exactly as on the Hiero side. The CLPR Service here is an ordinary contract, and the reference contracts also emit a log of the send that anyone can read.
reverse.protocol: The DATA message is appended under the next message id, its running hash is chained over its canonical protobuf payload bytes, and the next message id advances, as on every ledger: both sides store and hash the same encoding. The reference contracts also emit an event for the send.

reverse.label: QBFT proof
reverse.title: The EVM endpoint builds a QBFT state proof
reverse.plain: This ledger's validators seal each block header directly, so the endpoint pairs a sealed header with a proof of the contract storage holding the channel's state, to which the message is tied by the running hash.
reverse.protocol: The EVM endpoint reads one sealed block, which QBFT makes final, and builds every proof at it: the block header with its QBFT committed seals, the material that carries the validator set across any change since the peer's trust anchor, an account proof of the CLPR Service and storage proofs of the channel's state and, for a partial bundle, of the last message's running hash. The validator-change material depends on the channel's QBFT proof scheme: sealed headers at which the set changes, or proofs of a validator contract's storage.

reverse.label: gRPC open
reverse.title: A sync stream opens and BundleRequests are exchanged
reverse.plain: One sync session, with each side saying what it has already received. The transport does not care which way the message is going.
reverse.protocol: A sync cycle is one new bidirectional gRPC stream for one channel, opened by an initiator to an endpoint chosen from the peer manifest. Each side first sends a BundleRequest with its received message id, its channel status, the id of the trust anchor it holds and the manifest version it holds; each then answers the other with at most one bundle. Under the specification the stream runs over TLS when the responder's manifest entry carries a certificate, in plaintext otherwise, with no fallback and no client certificate; the reference endpoint serves it in plaintext. The request is unproven: it only shapes the bundle and never changes state.

reverse.label: gRPC send
reverse.title: The BundleResponse with the QBFT proof travels to the Hiero endpoint
reverse.plain: The bundle and its proof travel down the open stream to an endpoint of the Hiero ledger, one of its consensus nodes.
reverse.protocol: A BundleResponse carries one opaque bundle: the proven queue metadata, a contiguous run of messages, and the proof over the state of one sealed block.

reverse.label: pre-verify
reverse.title: The Hiero endpoint pre-verifies the bundle locally
reverse.plain: The receiving node is expected to check the bundle locally first, so it does not pay to submit anything it can see will be rejected.
reverse.protocol: Recommended practice on Hiero: the receiving node checks every bundle before submitting it, for the channel status, the size, local verification, the trust anchor and progress, and skips a bundle that makes no progress.

reverse.label: node submits
reverse.title: Bundle submission on the Hiero ledger
reverse.plain: The Hiero node hands the bundle to its own ledger. From here to the application call, everything runs inside that one transaction.
reverse.protocol: Recommended practice on Hiero: the receiving node submits the bundle as a node transaction paid by its node account, and the native CLPR Service processes it. The node is the submitter, so it receives the charges and penalties the bundle produces.

reverse.label: verify seals
reverse.title: QBFT committed seals verified against the trust anchor
reverse.plain: The Hiero ledger checks the seals on the block header against the validator set it holds for this channel. A quorum of the trusted validators must have sealed it: two thirds when the set is unchanged.
reverse.protocol: The channel's verifier on Hiero recovers the signers of the header's QBFT committed seals and requires a quorum of the trusted validator set among them, two thirds when the set is unchanged. When the set has changed since the trust anchor, the bundle carries the change: under the QBFT header scheme, each header at which the listed set changes, moving it by at most one member; under the QBFT contract scheme, each block at which the validator contract's set changes. Each must be sealed by enough of the set trusted before it, so history cannot be skipped; under the QBFT header scheme a header that changes the set by one member can need one signer fewer. The new set is returned as a trust anchor change.

reverse.label: verify proofs
reverse.title: Account and storage proofs verified
reverse.plain: Then it checks the proofs that tie the contract, and the channel's queue inside it, to that exact sealed block.
reverse.protocol: The account proof ties the CLPR Service contract, and its code hash, to the sealed header's state root; the storage proofs tie the channel's proven state, and for a partial bundle the last message's running hash, to that account. Every value comes from the one sealed block.

reverse.label: hash chain
reverse.title: Progress, replay and running-hash checks
reverse.plain: Then the bookkeeping. Does the bundle bring anything new? Do its messages follow on from the last one received, with no gap? Messages already received are skipped. Does recomputing the running hash give the proven value? Any mismatch and the whole bundle is rejected.
reverse.protocol: Bundle processing then checks, in order: the bundle's message count and each DATA payload are within the destination's own limits, its size having been checked before the verifier was called; at least one progress criterion holds; any new endpoint manifest and trust anchor are installed; the message range has no gap, and messages already received are skipped; the running hash recomputed from the stored received running hash over the new messages equals the proven running hash of the last one; and the acknowledgement neither moves backwards nor covers a message never sent. These are the CLPR Service's own checks; they catch verifier bugs, not a compromised verifier.

reverse.label: gas budget
reverse.title: Connector resolved and the gas budget computed
reverse.plain: The Hiero side looks up the connector that agreed to pay. Under the recommended design, it must be able to cover the worst-case charge before the application runs.
reverse.protocol: The message's connector id resolves to the local connector on the channel; a missing one gives CONNECTOR_NOT_FOUND. Recommended on Hiero: the worst-case charge is collected before dispatch and unused gas is refunded after, so a connector whose contract balance is below it is underfunded, is slashed, and gets CONNECTOR_UNDERFUNDED. The application gets a share of the transaction's remaining gas, split over the calls still to be made in the bundle, and at most the per-message limit.

reverse.label: onClprMessage()
reverse.title: The Hiero application receives the message and answers it
reverse.plain: The Hiero application receives the message and returns its answer. This is the crossing point for this direction.
reverse.protocol: The native CLPR Service calls the contract's onClprMessage with the channel id, the sender and the message data. A call that succeeds gives SUCCESS, with its returned bytes as the reply; a failed call, or return data that is not bytes, gives APPLICATION_ERROR with empty reply data. A gas budget of zero gives APPLICATION_ERROR with no call and no charge.

reverse.label: settle gas
reverse.title: The connector is charged and the submitter reimbursed
reverse.plain: Under the recommended design, the connector pays for the execution, with a margin, and the node that submitted the bundle receives the payment.
reverse.protocol: Recommended charging on Hiero: the execution cost is a flat per-message cost plus the cost of the gas the call used, and the margin applies to the flat part only. The CLPR Service transfers the charge directly from the connector contract's account to the submitting node; there is no administrator fallback.

reverse.label: reply queued
reverse.title: The reply is enqueued in the Hiero outbound queue
reverse.plain: The answer goes into the Hiero ledger's outbound queue for this channel, numbered and folded into its running hash the same way the original was.
reverse.protocol: A REPLY with the original message id, the status and the reply data is appended to the Hiero side's outbound queue and chained into its sent running hash, before the next message is processed. Every DATA message receives exactly one REPLY, in order.

reverse.label: received id
reverse.title: The Hiero side records how far it has received
reverse.plain: The Hiero side records how far it has received. The EVM ledger reads that number, proven, in the next bundle sent back, and uses it to know what it can delete.
reverse.protocol: After dispatch the Hiero side's received message id and received running hash advance to the bundle's last message. The next bundle to the EVM ledger proves them as queue metadata, and the EVM side takes that received message id as its acknowledgement.

reverse.label: threshold signature
reverse.title: The Hiero network signs the block root
reverse.plain: The return leg is proved with the Hiero nodes' joint signature over the block, the mechanism the other direction used on its way out.
reverse.protocol: Hiero nodes sign block roots with a hinTS threshold signature, valid only from nodes holding more than half of the consensus weight. Toward an EVM ledger the endpoint uses the hinTS proof scheme, anchored to the current hinTS verification key, and proves from the starting state of a directly signed, and so final, block.

reverse.label: gather proof
reverse.title: The Hiero endpoint gathers the reply and its proof
reverse.plain: The endpoint collects the proof tying the reply to that signed block, then sends it across; the receiving endpoint previews it before submitting.
reverse.protocol: The endpoint reads the channel record and the messages from one signed snapshot, with a Merkle path for each to the signed block root, and sends the bundle in a later sync cycle. Recommended practice: the EVM endpoint previews the submission against pending state and skips it if it would revert.

reverse.label: submitBundle()
reverse.title: The reply bundle lands on the EVM CLPR Service
reverse.plain: The reply is submitted on this ledger as an ordinary transaction. The reference contracts log an event when a bundle is processed in full.
reverse.protocol: Any account may call submitBundle with the channel id and the bundle. The reference contracts emit an event when the bundle is processed in full.

reverse.label: verifyBundle()
reverse.title: The verifier checks the threshold signature and the Merkle paths
reverse.plain: The verifier checks the Hiero nodes' joint signature and the proof paths against the signing key on record for this channel. If the network's roster has changed since, the bundle also proves the chain of keys from the recorded one to the new one. The endpoints that carried the bundle are trusted for none of it.
reverse.protocol: The CLPR Service calls the channel's verifier with the bundle, the stored trust anchor and the channel context; the call is read-only and the verifier keeps no per-channel state. Under the hinTS proof scheme the trust anchor names one hinTS verification key. The verifier checks the Merkle paths to the block root of the channel record, the last message and, when present, the endpoint manifest; the earlier messages are bound by the running hash. It checks the threshold signature on that root, which counts only from nodes holding more than half of the consensus weight. A bundle signed under a later key carries a provenance chain, each key signed by its predecessor; the verifier then returns a trust anchor change, stored before any message is processed. It returns the queue metadata, the messages, and the last message's id and running hash.

reverse.label: hash chain
reverse.title: Progress, replay and running-hash checks
reverse.plain: Sequence and running hash are checked before any reply is handed to an application, by the same algorithm as on the Hiero side.
reverse.protocol: Bundle processing then checks, in order: the bundle's message count and each DATA payload are within the destination's own limits, its size having been checked before the verifier was called; at least one progress criterion holds; any new endpoint manifest and trust anchor are installed; the message range has no gap, and messages already received are skipped; the running hash recomputed from the stored received running hash over the new messages equals the proven running hash of the last one; and the acknowledgement neither moves backwards nor covers a message never sent. These are the CLPR Service's own checks; they catch verifier bugs, not a compromised verifier.

reverse.label: ordering
reverse.title: Response ordering verified against the retained message
reverse.plain: Replies have to come back in the order the messages went out. If one arrives out of turn, nothing in that bundle is delivered and the channel pauses. It resumes by itself once a bundle arrives in the right order.
reverse.protocol: Every REPLY must answer the oldest unanswered DATA message in the outbound queue; the walk skips REPLY and CONTROL entries. A mismatch is a response ordering violation: nothing in the bundle is dispatched, an ACTIVE channel becomes PAUSED, and sends are rejected while queued messages keep syncing. The bundle's manifest and trust anchor changes still apply, and the CLPR Service may also apply its acknowledgement. The first bundle accepted without a violation returns the channel to ACTIVE.

reverse.label: onClprResponse()
reverse.title: The EVM application is called back
reverse.plain: The original contract is called back with the status and the other side's answer, closing the loop.
reverse.protocol: The CLPR Service calls onClprResponse on the original sender with the message id, the status and the reply data, but only if the sender is a contract. The call is best effort: a revert is ignored and the reply stays delivered. Under the recommended charging, the source connector pays for the gas the callback used; a failed charge is not slashed.

reverse.label: delivered
reverse.title: Reply delivered; the original message deleted
reverse.plain: The original message is deleted from the outbound queue now that its reply has arrived. In the reference contracts one transaction does all of it: it removes the message, calls the sending contract back, then announces the delivery on-chain.
reverse.protocol: The matched DATA message, kept past acknowledgement as the ordering reference, is deleted when its REPLY is processed. The reference contracts do this in the same transaction as the callback, in this order: they delete the queue entry, call onClprResponse, then emit a delivery event.

reverse.label: complete
reverse.title: Round trip complete
reverse.plain: The reverse journey closes the same way the forward one does, proved against each ledger's own consensus.
reverse.protocol: Two bundles, two proofs, two verifications, one reply. On the EVM side the reference contracts' events record the send and the delivery.
